column22: Using the frontend chatbox website helped me better understand SQL and schema design because it made the database feel connected to a real application. Instead of only writing queries and tables in isolation, we could see how the data we created was actually used by the app. For example, when messages were sent in the chat interface, they immediately appeared in the database tables. This helped me understand how the messages, channels, and channel_members tables were related and why certain columns were necessary. Seeing the app first retrieve data and the SQL backend actually save it allowed my team to fully understand what was going on. The chatbox website was especially helpful was when thinking about schema design for messages and channels. By interacting with the frontend, it became easier to see why channel_members needed to be a whole different table outside of just the need for normalization. This also helped reinforce the idea of using foreign keys as primary keys like username and channel_name to link tables together. It also helped me understand why queries needed to join multiple tables in order to answer questions about activity or interactions.

Start early and do not treat this project like a normal SQL worksheet. The hardest part is not just writing queries, but making your schema, constraints, and query outputs match the app.
Also, I would say that each milestone requires a different mindset, so do not approach the whole project the same way. For Milestone 1, take the design stage seriously. The project is very clear that good databases start with good design, and if you rush the ERD and constraints, you will end up rewriting tables later. This is the time to really understand cardinality, optionality, keys, and what rules should be enforced by the database.
For Milestone 4, test constantly in both pgAdmin and the app. This was probably the biggest shift in the project, because SQL stops being isolated practice and becomes the actual backend of the app. A query may look correct by itself but still fail if it does not match the app’s expected output exactly.

column22: One moment where the tool really helped me understand SQL and schema design was when I ran into an error saying that a query needed to return a column named “password.” I was confused at first because I knew my query was correctly pulling the password hash from the users table. After tracing the issue through SQL Lab, I realized the problem wasn’t the data itself, but that the app expected the column to be named exactly “password.” Fixing it by using password_hash AS password helped me understand how important it is for queries to match what the application expects, not just what makes sense in the database. It also showed me how SQL can be flexible without needing to change the entire schema. That moment made things click for me in terms of how the database and the app have to work closely together.

Using the tool to work on SQL and schema design really helped me understand how everything connects in a database. One moment that stood out was when I was creating tables and testing queries for a messaging system. Being able to run my SQL code and instantly see the results made a big difference. Instead of guessing whether my schema design was correct, I could immediately verify if the relationships between tables, like users, channels, and messages, were working as expected.
For example, when I created foreign keys to link tables together, I could quickly test joins and see if the data returned matched what I intended. If something was wrong, like missing data or incorrect relationships, I could go back, fix the schema, and rerun the query right away. This immediate feedback helped me understand not just how to write SQL, but why certain design choices matter.
Overall, the tool made the learning process more interactive and less frustrating. It helped me connect theory to practice by allowing me to experiment, make mistakes, and correct them in real time. This made me more confident in both SQL and schema design.

The most frustrating part was that the column names and table names kept being different or inconsistent. Sometimes I would write a query using what I thought was the correct column name, but it would not work because the actual name in the schema was slightly different. Even small differences like capitalization, underscores, or plural vs. singular names would cause errors, which made it hard to debug.
This was frustrating because the logic of my SQL query was often correct, but it would still fail due to naming mismatches. It took extra time to go back and check each table definition to make sure I was using the exact column names. Sometimes I also confused similar column names across different tables, which made joins more difficult than they needed to be.
However, this challenge helped me realize how important consistency is in schema design. Clear and standardized naming conventions make queries easier to write and understand. It also taught me to carefully read error messages and double-check the schema before assuming my query logic was wrong. In the end, even though it was frustrating, it improved my attention to detail and made me more precise when working with SQL.
column24:
One thing I didn’t expect to learn from this project was how much actual work goes into writing and refining SQL queries. At first, I thought queries would be straightforward—just selecting data from tables—but I quickly realized that even simple queries can take a lot of effort. You have to think carefully about how tables are connected, which joins to use, and how to filter or organize the data correctly.

I also learned that a lot of time is spent debugging and adjusting queries rather than writing them perfectly the first time. Small mistakes, like using the wrong column, forgetting a condition, or misunderstanding relationships between tables, can completely change the result. Because of this, I had to constantly test, revise, and improve my queries.

Another unexpected takeaway was how important planning is before writing the query. Understanding the schema and relationships ahead of time makes the process much smoother. Overall, this project showed me that SQL is not just about writing commands, but about problem-solving, attention to detail, and iteration.
